= Project References and Build
:description: TypeScript project references and build mode -- composite projects, tsc -b, .tsbuildinfo, incremental builds, source maps for debugging, compiler performance tooling, and type-checking alongside Babel, esbuild, SWC, and Vite.
:keywords: TypeScript project references, composite, tsc --build, tsc -b, tsbuildinfo, incremental, source maps, sourceRoot, mapRoot, enable-source-maps, generateTrace, skipLibCheck, import type, noEmit, esbuild, SWC, Babel, Vite
:page-aliases: web/typescript/project-references-and-build.adoc

include::partial$ai-disclaimer.adoc[]

A single `tsconfig.json` compiles one program. *Project references* let one `tsconfig.json` depend on
others, so a monorepo builds as a graph of small programs that each cache their own output. The
https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/project-references.html[Project References] handbook chapter is
the companion to this page; what follows is the working summary, plus how to keep type-checking honest when
another tool does the actual emit.

== composite, references, and tsc -b

A referenced project must set `composite: true` (which forces `declaration: true` and a rootDir), and the
depending project lists it under `references`. `tsc -b` (alias for `tsc --build`) then topologically sorts
the graph, skips projects whose inputs are unchanged, and builds the rest in order.

A concrete monorepo: `packages/core` (no deps), `packages/api` (depends on `core`), `packages/web`
(depends on `core` and `api`).

[source,json]
----
// tsconfig.base.json -- shared compiler options
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "sourceMap": true,
    "composite": true,
    "incremental": true
  }
}
----

[source,json]
----
// packages/core/tsconfig.json -- a leaf, no references
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src" },
  "include": ["src"]
}

// packages/api/tsconfig.json -- adds one reference
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src" },
  "include": ["src"],
  "references": [{ "path": "../core" }]
}

// packages/web/tsconfig.json -- depends on both
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src" },
  "include": ["src"],
  "references": [{ "path": "../core" }, { "path": "../api" }]
}
----

[source,json]
----
// tsconfig.json at the repo root -- a "solution" file that builds everything
{
  "files": [],
  "references": [
    { "path": "packages/core" },
    { "path": "packages/api" },
    { "path": "packages/web" }
  ]
}
----

[source,bash]
----
# Build the whole graph in dependency order, skipping unchanged projects.
npx tsc -b

# Same thing, targeting one leaf -- its dependencies are built first as needed.
npx tsc -b packages/web

# Show what would be built and why, without writing anything.
npx tsc -b --dry

# Explain each up-to-date / out-of-date decision.
npx tsc -b --verbose

# Delete every project's outputs and .tsbuildinfo files.
npx tsc -b --clean

# Rebuild-on-change across the whole graph.
npx tsc -b --watch
----

Import across packages by their package name (`+import { x } from "@scope/core"+`), not by relative path into
`dist`; `declarationMap: true` makes editor "Go to Definition" jump to the dependency's `.ts` source rather
than its emitted `.d.ts`. Package-name resolution is a xref:programming-languages/typescript/modules.adoc[modules] concern --
each `package.json` needs `"main"`/`"exports"` pointing at `dist`.

=== .tsbuildinfo and incremental

`incremental: true` writes a `.tsbuildinfo` file (next to `outDir`, or at
`tsBuildInfoFile`) recording file hashes and the last program's signatures. The next run reads it and
recompiles only what changed. `composite: true` implies `incremental: true`, so every referenced project
gets this cache for free; a standalone project can opt in with just `incremental` and no references.

[source,bash]
----
# First build: full compile.
npx tsc -b --verbose
#   [projects] building packages/core, packages/api, packages/web

# Touch one file in core, build again:
npx tsc -b --verbose
#   project 'packages/core' is out of date because ... -- rebuilds core
#   project 'packages/api' is out of date because output of 'core' changed
#   project 'packages/web' ... likewise
# Unchanged projects report "up to date" and are skipped.
----

Commit-time or CI caching of `.tsbuildinfo` (or restoring `outDir` + `.tsbuildinfo` from a cache key) turns
a cold `tsc -b` into a near-no-op when nothing changed. Delete the file (or `tsc -b --clean`) if incremental
state ever looks stale.

== Source maps for debugging

`sourceMap: true` emits a `.js.map` beside each `.js` so debuggers show your `.ts`. Two path knobs matter
when the served layout differs from the build layout: `sourceRoot` prefixes every source path recorded in
the map (point it at where the browser or editor can fetch the `.ts` files), and `mapRoot` tells the
emitted `.js` where its `.map` lives (via the `+//# sourceMappingURL=+` comment) when the map is served from a
different directory than the script.

[source,json]
----
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "sourceMap": true,
    "sourceRoot": "/@src",          // browser resolves original sources under this URL
    "mapRoot": "/maps",             // .js files point their sourceMappingURL here
    "inlineSources": true           // embed the .ts text in the map -- no separate fetch
  }
}
----

For the browser, ship the `.map` files (or use `inlineSourceMap`) and enable "Enable JavaScript source
maps" in DevTools; breakpoints then bind to `.ts`. Bundlers usually take over source-map generation -- see
_Building with other tools_ below.

For Node, run with `--enable-source-maps` so stack traces point at `.ts` lines and columns:

[source,bash]
----
# Node applies the .js.map files at runtime; no extra deps.
node --enable-source-maps dist/api/server.js

# Also honored via env var (useful in Docker / process managers):
NODE_OPTIONS=--enable-source-maps node dist/api/server.js
----

`declarationMap: true` is the type-level counterpart: it maps `.d.ts` back to `.ts` so cross-project "Go to
Definition" and refactors land in source.

== Compiler performance

When `tsc` feels slow, measure before changing anything.

[source,bash]
----
# High-level counts: files, lines, symbols, memory, and phase timings.
npx tsc --noEmit --diagnostics

# Adds parse/bind/check/emit breakdown and I/O read/write times.
npx tsc --noEmit --extendedDiagnostics

# Emit a trace/ directory: trace.<n>.json (load in chrome://tracing or
# https://ui.perfetto.dev) plus types.<n>.json for the type registry.
npx tsc --noEmit --generateTrace trace

# Analyze the trace for the most expensive type instantiations.
npx analyze-trace trace
----

Common wins:

* `skipLibCheck: true` -- skip type-checking of all `.d.ts` (yours are still checked on emit). Almost always
  worth it; it removes conflicting/expensive `@types` from the check.
* Keep types *shallow*. Deep conditional and mapped-type recursion, huge union types, and large inferred
  object literals dominate check time; give hot paths explicit, named types instead of letting the compiler
  synthesize giant structural ones.
* `+import type { Foo }+` / `+import { type Foo }+` -- mark type-only imports so they carry no runtime edge and
  cannot drag a module into the JS graph. See xref:programming-languages/typescript/tsconfig-and-compiler-options.adoc[tsconfig
  and compiler options] for `verbatimModuleSyntax`, which enforces this.
* Project references themselves -- a change in `packages/web` no longer re-checks `packages/core`.

The native port (the "7.0" TypeScript compiler, `tsc` rewritten in Go) runs project loads and type-checking
roughly *10x faster* than the current JavaScript implementation with the *same* type system and semantics --
same `tsconfig.json`, same errors. It is a drop-in speedup, not a language change.

== Building with other tools

Babel, esbuild, SWC, and Vite compile TypeScript by *stripping* type annotations per file -- they are fast
precisely because they do *no* type-checking and never load the full program. They will happily emit code
that `tsc` would reject. The rule: let the bundler emit, and run `tsc --noEmit` as a separate gate in CI.

[source,json]
----
// package.json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build",
    "typecheck": "tsc -b --noEmit",
    "test": "vitest run",
    "ci": "npm run typecheck && npm run build && npm run test"
  }
}
----

[source,bash]
----
# esbuild / SWC / Babel: transpile only, zero type errors reported.
npx esbuild src/index.ts --bundle --sourcemap --outfile=dist/index.js
npx swc src -d dist --source-maps
npx babel src --extensions .ts,.tsx --out-dir dist --source-maps

# The type-check that none of the above perform -- keep it in CI.
npx tsc -b --noEmit          # whole reference graph
npx tsc --noEmit --watch     # local feedback loop while the bundler serves

# Vite: `vite build` never type-checks; wire tsc alongside it.
npx vite build && npx tsc -b --noEmit
----

Because these transpilers see one file at a time, constructs that need type information fail or misbehave:
`const enum` inlining, legacy `experimentalDecorators` metadata, and namespace merging. Prefer plain
`enum` or literal unions, standard decorators, and ES modules. `isolatedModules: true` in `tsconfig.json`
makes `tsc` flag exactly these single-file-unsafe patterns. See
xref:programming-languages/javascript/tooling-babel.adoc[Babel] and
xref:programming-languages/javascript/tooling-bundling-npm-publishing.adoc[bundling and npm publishing] for the JS-side
setup, and the
https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/integrating-with-build-tools.html[Integrating with Build
Tools] handbook page for per-tool plugins. Watch-mode tuning (polling, excluded directories) is covered in
https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/configuring-watch.html[Configuring Watch].

== A two-project build you can run

The sections above describe the pieces; this one builds the smallest real example and shows exactly what `tsc -b`
prints, so that its messages are familiar before they appear in a large repository. The layout is a `core` package that
holds the `RequestState` type from the xref:programming-languages/typescript/worked-example.adoc[worked example], an `api`
package that uses it, and a root solution file:

[source,text]
----
mono/
  package.json                { "type": "module" }
  tsconfig.base.json          shared options
  tsconfig.json               solution file: builds nothing itself
  packages/
    core/  tsconfig.json  src/state.ts
    api/   tsconfig.json  src/main.ts
----

`tsconfig.base.json` holds what both projects share:

[source,json]
----
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}
----

Each package marks itself `composite` and sets `rootDir` and `outDir`. `api` additionally declares the dependency on
`core` under `references`:

[source,json]
----
// packages/core/tsconfig.json
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "composite": true, "rootDir": "src", "outDir": "dist" },
  "include": ["src"]
}

// packages/api/tsconfig.json
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "composite": true, "rootDir": "src", "outDir": "dist" },
  "include": ["src"],
  "references": [{ "path": "../core" }]
}

// tsconfig.json (the solution file)
{ "files": [], "references": [{ "path": "packages/core" }, { "path": "packages/api" }] }
----

The solution file has an empty `files` list on purpose: it compiles nothing and only gives `tsc -b` a single entry point
that lists every project. The sources:

[source,typescript]
----
// packages/core/src/state.ts
export type RequestState<T> =
  | { readonly kind: "idle" }
  | { readonly kind: "success"; readonly data: T }
  | { readonly kind: "error"; readonly error: string };
export function describe<T>(s: RequestState<T>): string { return s.kind; }

// packages/api/src/main.ts
import { describe, type RequestState } from "../../core/src/state.js";
const s: RequestState<number> = { kind: "success", data: 1 };
console.log(describe(s));
----

Notice that `main.ts` imports `core`&#39;s *source* path. Because of the reference, the compiler redirects the import to
`core`&#39;s generated declaration file, so `api` is checked against `core`&#39;s public types and not against its
implementation.

== What `tsc -b --verbose` prints

The first build has no cache, so both projects build, in dependency order:

[source,console]
----
$ npx tsc -b --verbose
Projects in this build:
    * packages/core/tsconfig.json
    * packages/api/tsconfig.json
    * tsconfig.json

Project 'packages/core/tsconfig.json' is out of date because output file 'packages/core/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo' does not exist
Building project '.../packages/core/tsconfig.json'...
Project 'packages/api/tsconfig.json' is out of date because output file 'packages/api/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo' does not exist
Building project '.../packages/api/tsconfig.json'...
----

(Each line is prefixed with a timestamp in real output.) Running it again changes nothing, and says so:

[source,console]
----
Project 'packages/core/tsconfig.json' is up to date because newest input 'packages/core/src/state.ts' is older than output 'packages/core/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo'
Project 'packages/api/tsconfig.json' is up to date because newest input 'packages/api/src/main.ts' is older than output 'packages/api/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo'
----

The interesting case is a change in `core`. The two edits below behave differently. A *body-only* edit (here, appending a
comment) rebuilds `core` but leaves its public declarations unchanged, so `api` does not need re-checking:

[source,console]
----
Project 'packages/core/tsconfig.json' is out of date because output 'packages/core/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo' is older than input 'packages/core/src/state.ts'
Building project '.../packages/core/tsconfig.json'...
Project 'packages/api/tsconfig.json' is up to date with .d.ts files from its dependencies
Updating output timestamps of project '.../packages/api/tsconfig.json'...
----

A *signature* change (adding a `"loading"` arm to the union) changes `core`&#39;s declaration output, and `api` is rebuilt:

[source,console]
----
Project 'packages/core/tsconfig.json' is out of date because output 'packages/core/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo' is older than input 'packages/core/src/state.ts'
Building project '.../packages/core/tsconfig.json'...
Project 'packages/api/tsconfig.json' is out of date because output 'packages/api/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo' is older than input 'packages/core'
Building project '.../packages/api/tsconfig.json'...
----

[mermaid]
....
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as You edit core/src/state.ts
    participant B as tsc -b
    participant C as core project
    participant A as api project
    Dev->>B: tsc -b
    B->>C: input newer than tsbuildinfo? yes, rebuild
    C-->>B: new dist/*.d.ts + tsbuildinfo
    B->>A: did core's .d.ts change?
    alt declarations unchanged (body edit)
        A-->>B: up to date, only touch timestamps
    else declarations changed (signature edit)
        B->>A: rebuild and re-check against new types
    end
....

This is the reason the pattern pays off in a big monorepo: the cost of a change is proportional to how much of the
*public surface* it touches, not to how many files exist. After the builds, the generated files sit next to each
project:

[source,text]
----
packages/api/dist/main.d.ts            (and main.js)
packages/api/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo
packages/core/dist/state.d.ts          (and state.js)
packages/core/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo
----

== Errors you meet when the setup is wrong

Three mistakes account for nearly every failure when adopting references, and each has a distinctive code.

*A referenced project that is not `composite`* (here `core` loses `"composite": true`):

[source,console]
----
packages/api/tsconfig.json(5,18): error TS6306: Referenced project '.../packages/core' must have setting "composite": true.
----

*A source file outside the project's `include`*, here `api` importing a file from `core` that `core` does not list in
its `include` (`packages/core/extra/x.ts`):

[source,console]
----
packages/api/src/other.ts(1,19): error TS6059: File '.../packages/core/extra/x.ts' is not under 'rootDir' '.../packages/api/src'. 'rootDir' is expected to contain all source files.
packages/api/src/other.ts(1,19): error TS6307: File '.../packages/core/extra/x.ts' is not listed within the file list of project '.../packages/api/tsconfig.json'. Projects must list all files or use an 'include' pattern.
----

The fix is to include the file in `core` (and import it through `core`&#39;s public entry), never to widen `api`&#39;s `rootDir`.

*Combining incompatible flags.* `tsc -b` is a different mode with its own rules: for example `--clean` cannot be
combined with `--verbose`, and it reports the pair as an error:

[source,console]
----
$ npx tsc -b --clean --verbose
error TS6370: Options 'clean' and 'verbose' cannot be combined.
----

Run `npx tsc -b --clean` alone to delete the outputs of every project in the graph, and then build again when an
incremental state looks wrong. In CI, restoring `dist` and every `.tsbuildinfo` from a cache keyed on the lock file
and sources turns the first, no-op `tsc -b` into the "up to date" lines shown above.

== The build graph

`tsc -b` walks `references` depth-first, builds each project only after its dependencies, and skips any
whose `.tsbuildinfo` says its inputs are unchanged.

[mermaid]
....
flowchart BT
    core["packages/core<br/>composite: true"]
    api["packages/api<br/>references: core"]
    web["packages/web<br/>references: core, api"]
    root["tsconfig.json (solution)<br/>files: [], references: all"]

    core --> api
    core --> web
    api --> web
    web --> root

    subgraph order["tsc -b build order"]
        direction LR
        s1["1. core"] --> s2["2. api"] --> s3["3. web"]
    end
....
